item.title: Chemical Biology in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: From Ligand Discovery to Virtual Cells.
item.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how scientists, including chemical biologists, conduct research. This review is intended to serve as an introduction for chemical biologists to applications of artificial intelligence in chemical biology. We review how chemical and biological data are featurized, the types of models commonly used in chemical biology applications, challenges in assessing accuracy of artificial intelligence models, and recent developments in agentic artificial intelligence for autonomous research. The applications we will cover include protein structure prediction, ligand discovery, peptide and protein design, prediction of mutational effects, interactomics and gene regulation, and virtual cells.

item.title: Scalable and Sustainable Synthesis of Long Single-Stranded DNA for Emerging Biological Applications.
item.abstract: ssDNA greater than 200 nts, or long ssDNA (lssDNA), has become indispensable across genome editing, synthetic biology, and DNA nanotechnology, yet its production has remained limited by cost, sequence length, and environmental burden. A new generation of technologies is beginning to shift these constraints. Chemical synthesis is steadily improving in efficiency and sustainability, enzymatic methods are expanding the achievable length and sequence flexibility of lssDNA, and emerging in vivo systems promise high yield production with minimal cost and resource wastes. These advances collectively move lssDNA from a specialized, hard to obtain material toward a broadly accessible tool. This review brings these developments together to highlight the principles behind their progress and the opportunities they create for scalable, programmable, and sustainable lssDNA manufacturing.

item.title: Calculation of sequence space coverage in a mutagenesis library.
item.abstract: Directed evolution requires screening of large mutagenesis libraries, but accurate calculation of library sizes needed to discover functional variants remains challenging. Existing models provide baseline estimates, yet current computational approaches for finding the best variants scale poorly with library complexity. Here, we introduce a scalable computational framework that overcomes the combinatorial scaling bottlenecks of previous top-k models. By aggregating variants into a composition log-sum distribution and applying log-space convolution across randomisation blocks, we extend coverage estimation to massive sequence spaces and mixed codon schemes. By inverting these calculations, we establish conservative screening upper bounds and practical ceilings on the maximum randomisable positions for experimental design. Ultimately, this framework provides a rapid, quantitative tool to balance the statistical coverage-diversity trade-off within the limitations of laboratory screening. Finally, this is implemented as an open-source web application (SSCC), publicly available at https://florez-alberto.github.io/SSCC/, that allows researchers to construct heterogeneous library designs and compute required sampling depths, coverage probabilities, and absolute randomisation limits.

item.title: PRIZM: combining low-N data and zero-shot models to design enhanced protein variants.
item.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Machine learning has repeatedly shown the ability to accelerate protein engineering, but many approaches demand large amounts of robust, high-quality training data as well as substantial computational expertise. While large pre-trained models can function as zero-shot proxies for predicting variant effects, selecting the best model for a given protein property is often non-trivial.
RESULTS: Here, we introduce Protein Ranking using Informed Zero-shot Modelling (PRIZM), a two-phase workflow that first uses a high-quality low-N dataset to identify the most suitable pre-trained zero-shot model for a target protein property and then applies that model to rank and prioritize an in silico variant library for experimental testing. Across diverse benchmark datasets spanning multiple protein properties, PRIZM reliably separated low- from high-performing models using datasets of ∼20 labelled variants. We further demonstrate PRIZM in enzyme engineering case studies targeting sucrose synthase thermostability and glycosyltransferase activity, where PRIZM-guided selection identified improved variants, including gains of ∼3°C in apparent melting temperature and ∼20% higher relative activity. PRIZM provides an accessible, data-efficient route to leverage foundation models for protein design while requiring minimal experimental data.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: PRIZM is publicly available via Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23035983, and the PRIZM GitHub repository https://github.com/daha-la/PRIZM.
item.authors: Harding-Larsen, Lax, Escorial García, et al.

item.title: Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 as a Programmable Bridge Chassis for Biomanufacturing and Host-Responsive Living Systems.
item.abstract: Microbial biomanufacturing and engineered probiotics increasingly use related microbial lineages across distinct product architectures, but the associated engineering and evidence requirements are rarely compared. Here, Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) is evaluated as a programmable bridge chassis across four alternative deployment modes: purified molecule, cell-derived architecture/material, living-cell product, and host-state-responsive living system. The review links carbon-nitrogen-energy-redox allocation and global regulation to cellular-state trajectories, interface capacity, safety refactoring, materials-assisted protection, containment, and mode-specific qualification. Direct evidence includes 100-L heparosan fermentation, antibiotic-free β-alanine production, engineered outer-membrane-vesicle delivery, human studies of phenylalanine-consuming EcN, and glucose-responsive GLP-1 delivery in diabetic mice and non-human primates. The terminated SYNB1934 Phase 3 program is considered alongside positive studies to distinguish proof of function, pharmacodynamic activity, tolerability, manufacturing readiness, and late-stage efficacy. Operational criteria for bridge-chassis designation, explicit rules for boundary cases, and a prospective design-build-test-learn agenda are proposed. As functional embodiment changes, engineering priorities shift among flux, state, interface, formulation, containment, and evidence-not necessarily toward a more advanced mode.

item.title: A synNotch-based morphogen detection system reveals sFRP2 enhances Wnt3a signaling.
item.abstract: Morphogen gradients provide essential positional information during tissue development, yet the extracellular mechanisms that regulate morphogen transport remain elusive. Here, we introduce a mechanosensitive detection system based on synthetic Notch (synNotch) receptors that selectively detect surface-bound morphogens. Applying this platform to Wnt signaling, we demonstrate that secreted Frizzled-related protein 2 (sFRP2) promotes the recruitment of Wnt3a to the cell surface via heparan sulfate proteoglycans, enabling robust activation of canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Notably, sFRP2 extends the effective signaling range of Wnt3a under ligand-limiting conditions. In intestinal organoid cultures, sFRP2 enhances Wnt3a-driven growth and induces high-Wnt morphological states even at low Wnt3a concentrations. These findings identify sFRP2 as an extracellular carrier that stabilizes surface-bound Wnt3a and regulates both the strength and spatial range of Wnt signaling. Broadly, this work demonstrates the utility of synNotch mechano-sensing for dissecting extracellular morphogen dynamics and highlights the potential of morphogen carrier proteins to optimize organoid culture.

item.title: Advancing Engineered Living Hydrogels Using Cell-Node Crosslinking.
item.abstract: Engineered living hydrogels (ELHs) represent a convergence between biomaterial science and synthetic biology, wherein living and non-living components are combined to overcome the limitations of traditional hydrogels. While early ELHs relied on passive cell encapsulation, the next-generation of ELHs, cell-node hydrogels (CNGels), employ cells as active crosslinking nodes, fundamentally transforming hydrogel functionality and performance. This strategy enables dynamic bioactive properties, including self-healing, self-growing, self-degrading, and real-time programmable behavior through cellular sensing and adaptation. These CNGels have been successfully engineered using both mammalian and non-mammalian cells by employing a variety of strategies from metabolic glycoengineering and bioorthogonal click chemistry to SpyTag/SpyCatcher-mediated assembly, enabling a wide range of biomedical applications from tissue engineering and regenerative medicine to bioremediation. This review highlights the current fabrication strategies and mechanistic principles of CNGels, as well as provides a forward-looking perspective on optimizing CNGels for clinical and industrial deployment.

item.title: Genome-wide synthetic engineering identifies essential genes and host-specific factors governing tropism switching in mycobacteriophage D29.
item.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Mycobacteriophage D29 is a phage that infects mycobacteria and has been studied as a model since its isolation in 1954. It can infect multiple species, including Mycobacterium smegmatis, nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), and Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis. D29 is now considered a potential candidate for NTM and tuberculosis treatment. However, 34% of its genes remain functionally uncharacterized. Recent advances in synthetic biology have enabled efficient phage engineering, reducing the challenges of mutant screening in bulk populations. In this study, we generated a set of single-gene deletion mutants using synthetic engineering techniques to identify genes required for phage propagation. Functional analysis of all 77 genes showed that 44 genes (57%) and all tRNAs were nonessential for phage replication. Furthermore, infection assays using the deletion mutants demonstrated that genes 55, 56, and 59 are required for efficient infection of M. tuberculosis H37Rv but are dispensable for infection of M. smegmatis, highlighting their contribution to host-specific phage infectivity. These findings provide valuable insights into D29 biology and phage-host dynamics.
IMPORTANCE: In this study, we employed synthetic biology techniques to construct a comprehensive library of the gene and tRNA deletion mutants of mycobacteriophage D29 to systematically assess gene essentiality. Notably, over half of the genes were found to be nonessential for the lytic cycle, suggesting potential roles in environmental adaptation and host-mycobacteria interactions. Furthermore, we found that the D29Δ55, D29Δ56, and D29Δ59 mutants showed markedly reduced plating efficiency on Mycobacterium tuberculosis although these genes were dispensable for infection of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Such differential genetic requirements highlight their potential roles in modulating phage-host interactions across distinct Mycobacterium species. These findings provide valuable insights into the functional genomics of D29 and phage biology and support its continued development as a candidate for phage-based therapies against nontuberculous mycobacteria and M. tuberculosis infections.

item.title: Engineering Silk and Silk-like Proteins into High-Performance Fiber Materials.
item.abstract: Silk and silk-like proteins emerge as programmable building blocks for high-performance fiber materials because they can integrate mechanical robustness, biological compatibility, environmental responsiveness, and degradability within genetically defined polymers. Synthetic biology now enables precise control over protein sequence, repeat number, molecular weight, and modular architecture, creating opportunities to design fibers beyond naturally harvested silks. However, application-ready protein fibers require coordinated control across multiple length scales, from sequence-encoded motifs and molecular assembly to spinning-induced alignment, hierarchical network formation, and final property profiles. This review discusses recent advances in engineering silk and silk-like proteins into mechanically and functionally optimized fibers. We highlight how crystallite-forming motifs, amorphous domains, terminal domains, and folded or dynamic modules contribute to fiber strength, toughness, extensibility, damping, shape recovery, humidity stability, biodegradation, and recyclability. We further connect these sequence-structure-property relationships to applications in structural textiles, biomedical fibers, smart and protective systems, and sustainable materials. Finally, we discuss future opportunities in scalable recombinant production and data-driven sequence design. These advances are expected to accelerate the translation of engineered protein fibers into practical high-performance materials.

item.title: Nanoparticle therapeutics for infectious diseases integrating AI-guided design, crispr delivery, phage synergy, and immune modulation.
item.abstract: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

item.title: VP2-TALE fusions increase AAV2 capsid filling with payload bearing cognate TALE target sequences as determined by qPCR/ELISA.
item.abstract: We sought to improve the empty/full ratio of recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (AAV2) production by engineering the capsid to increase the favorability of its interactions with payload genomes. We fused a transcription activator-like effector (TALE), sequence-specific DNA-binding domain to the VP2 protein (VP2-TALE), either directly or via flexible linkers, within a transgene encoded by an overexpression plasmid. We also engineered seven different versions of the green fluorescent protein (GFP) payload plasmid, with up to three copies of a 14 base-pair TALE-cognate target sequence. Co-transfection with a helper plasmid, a RepCap plasmid engineered to prevent native VP2 expression, and a VP2-TALE expression plasmid resulted in lower capsid titers and higher viral genome titers when TALE target sequences were present in the payload plasmid than in control transfections in which the payload lacked TALE target sequences. Western blotting with an anti-VP antibody showed VP-positive proteins of the size predicted for VP2-TALE fusion. Electron microscopy indicated the presence of correctly formed viral capsids. ELISA and qPCR analysis indicated that these transfections could result in increases in capsid filling approaching 200%.

item.title: Engineered plant-microbe symbiosis enables aerobic upcycling of wastewater heavy metal into photosynthetic semiconductor biohybrids.
item.abstract: Plants naturally extract heavy metals from polluted water, but they merely accumulate these toxins in their tissues, leaving behind hazardous biomass. Alternatively, microbial biomineralization can precipitate dissolved metals into valuable semiconductor nanomaterials, but this process relies on sulfate-reducing bacteria, strict anaerobes that cannot survive the oxygen-rich environment of plant roots. Here we overcome this oxygen limitation by engineering the aerobic bacterium Vibrio natriegens to colonize water lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) roots and assemble metal sulfides directly in the rhizosphere. Sustained entirely by root exudates, the bacteria perform aerobic sulfate reduction to generate hydrogen sulfide, precipitating aqueous cadmium and lead into cell-surface-anchored CdS and PbS semiconductor nanoparticles (4.94-11.00 nm). The resulting semiconductor-cell biohybrids exhibit photoelectric properties, making them valuable for post-harvest applications such as solar-driven biosynthesis. Concurrently, bacterial auxin secretion buffers the host plant against metal toxicity, recovering root biomass by over 10%. Over consecutive treatment cycles, this system removed 30% of cadmium and 63% of lead from the aqueous phase, far exceeding the capacity of single-host controls. By decoupling sulfide biomineralization from anaerobic constraints, this rhizospheric strategy upgrades wastewater treatment from metal sequestration to optoelectronic material recovery.

item.title: RNA Therapeutics in Cardiovascular Medicine: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Practice.
item.abstract: RNA therapeutics are an exciting class of medications that target RNA and/or are themselves made from RNA. Most RNA therapeutics that have been approved for clinical use are antisense oligonucleotides or small interfering RNAs. To date, eight RNA therapeutics with cardiovascular relevance have received US Food and Drug Administration approval, but not all of them have specific indications for treating cardiovascular disease. There is a promising pipeline of additional cardiovascular RNA therapies targeting lipoprotein(a), angiopoietin-like protein 3, and angiotensinogen. Chemical modifications to therapeutic nucleic acids are important for conferring nuclease resistance and limiting immunostimulation in vivo, and enhanced delivery can be achieved using N-acetylgalactosamine conjugation and/or lipid nanoparticles. Emerging approaches include stereopure oligonucleotide chemistry, circular RNAs, adenosine-to-inosine RNA base editing, and nonhepatic targeting. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of each modality, the clinical evidence for approved cardiovascular RNA therapeutics, selected pipeline candidates in advanced trials, and directions for future development.

item.title: Redesigning photoprotection: nature-inspired and synthetic biology strategies to enhance crop productivity.
item.abstract: Photosynthesis captures solar energy and carbon dioxide to fuel life on Earth by providing food and oxygen. When light intensity exceeds photosynthetic capacity, resulting in the saturation of the electron transport chain, photosynthetic organisms protect themselves by activating photoprotective non-photochemical quenching (NPQ), which dissipates excess energy as heat. Despite the importance of NPQ in plant physiology, its slow activation and relaxation may cause substantial yield losses in field-grown crops. For this reason, qE, the fastest component of NPQ, has become a central biotechnological target for crop engineering. While pioneering approaches, such as the "VPZ strategy" involving the overexpression of both xanthophyll cycle and PSBS proteins, have successfully enhanced field productivity, their efficacy varies across species, highlighting current biotechnological bottlenecks. This review discusses the molecular bases and activation models of qE in different clades, describing the transition from LHCSR- to PSBS-dependent strategies and the central role of the xanthophyll cycle, while highlighting open debates and unresolved questions. Further, it outlines the future of NPQ engineering, exploring nature-inspired solutions, including the heterologous expression of LHCSR or alternative xanthophyll cycles in crops. Finally, this review discusses how CRISPR-Cas9-driven precision breeding and the application of Artificial Intelligence, and de novo protein design will guide future biotechnological intervention toward developing high-yielding, better resource-efficient crops.

item.title: Cell-free reconstitution reveals synergistic stabilization of microtubule doublets by PACRG and FAP20.
item.abstract: Ciliary microtubule doublets, consisting of an incomplete B-tubule on the surface of a complete A-microtubule, form the fundamental structural framework of motile and sensory cilia/flagella. Ciliary proteins PACRG and FAP20, which are essential for flagellar stability and function, localize to the junction between the A- and the B-tubule. However, their precise role in microtubule doublet assembly and dynamics remains unknown. Here, using a cell-free assay, TIRF-microscopy, and cryo-electron tomography, we demonstrate that in combination PACRG and FAP20 stabilize B-tubule dynamics and microtubule doublet architecture. We show that together these proteins localize to the B-tubules in distinct, high-density patches, which locally stabilize B-tubule by decreasing its depolymerization velocity and increasing its rescue frequency. Cryo-tomography of in vitro reconstructed microtubule doublets in presence of PACRG and FAP20 reveals reduced B-tubule curvature fluctuations, promoting a more rigid and aligned conformation. Altogether, our findings suggest that PACRG and FAP20 function synergistically to reinforce microtubule doublet stability, ensuring ciliary integrity and function.
